The CBD is built on stable rock: 400-million-year-old mudstone on the eastern half and volcanic basalt on the western half, with Elizabeth Street roughly marking the boundary.

Flea from the Red Hot Chili Peppers was born in Melbourne.

Melbourne was briefly named Batmania before being renamed.

The Montague Street Bridge has its own website tracking incidents, including a 'days since last hit' counter.

Punt Road was named after the punt boats that were once the only way to cross the river there.
Rocky Road chocolate was invented in Melbourne, sold to miners heading up the 'rocky road' to Ballarat.
Queen Victoria Market is built on top of a cemetery; about 1,000 bodies were reinterred, but many remain buried underneath the carpark.
The first building connected to Melbourne's sewer system in 1897 was a pub in Port Melbourne.
The term 'Buckley's chance' originates from the Buckley & Nunn department store in Bourke Street, not the convict William Buckley.
From 2011 to 2017, Melbourne was voted the most liveable city in the world for seven consecutive years.
Melbourne is built on a swamp.

Melbourne has the second-largest Greek population in the world, behind Athens.
The federal parliament used to sit in Melbourne while Canberra was being built.

Melbourne's CBD grid is almost the same layout as the free tram zone.
The Queen Victoria Market was built on top of Melbourne's first cemetery, with hundreds of bodies buried beneath it.
A small waterfall on the Yarra River near Queen Street was demolished in 1883.
Fed Square has a giant underground labyrinth that regulates temperature and provides free cooling to The Atrium.
Melbourne has produced the most #1 overall NBA draft picks of any city, including Andrew Bogut, Kyrie Irving, and Ben Simmons.
Melbourne is the only place in the world where people 'barrack' for a sporting team, a term derived from military teams like the Collingwood Rifles.
Melbourne has the biggest tram system in the world.
The main reason Melbourne became the capital instead of Geelong is that city officials made fake maps showing Melbourne's port was closer to the goldfields, diverting miners there.

In 2017, a subterranean neighbourhood the size of five tennis courts was discovered near Wesley Church on Lonsdale Street, buried in the 1850s when the Lonsdale Swamp was paved over to raise the street level by two metres.
'Moomba' actually means 'up your bum' in Koori and was suggested as a joke.
The pond in the Botanic Gardens is a natural bend of the Yarra River that was redirected to its current course.
The four lions on the Shrine of Remembrance commemorate the penny drive children of Melbourne participated in to fund the shrine, with cherubs holding bandoliers of pennies.
There used to be a train line to Springvale Cemetery with specific cars to transport dead bodies to the necropolis.
Elizabeth Street used to be a creek and still floods from time to time because water runs beneath it.
Several public toilets and urinals around the city are heritage listed.

In 1934, Melbourne City Council organised an international air race from England to Melbourne with the finish line down the straight at Flemington Race Course, drawing worldwide attention during the Great Depression.
The Bolte Bridge is actually two separate bridges, one northbound and one southbound, held up by separate pillars.
The world's first feature film was filmed and shown in Melbourne.

The Scenic Railway roller coaster at Luna Park, built in 1912, is the oldest continuously operated roller coaster in the world.
Up until the 1960s, hook turns were compulsory at every intersection with traffic lights in Melbourne.
The 1969 Melbourne Transport Plan recommended a massive grid of freeways, most of which were cancelled by Premier Rupert Hamer.
There was a theme park in Cremorne that closed in 1863, and Cremorne only officially became a suburb in 1999.
Advance Australia Fair was written by Peter McCormick on a bus on the way home from the Exhibition Centre.

A known serial killer from the UK, a key suspect in the Jack the Ripper murders, moved to Australia, murdered a lady, and buried her under a hearthstone in Windsor before being hanged at the Old Melbourne Gaol.
Melbourne has the largest Greek population of any city outside Athens.
The city's Chinatown is called that because it's where Chinese people settled, lived, and worked, not just a restaurant district.
The original plan for the Arts Centre had the spire on the ground and theatres underground, but it couldn't be built that way because the land is too swampy.
There used to be an outer loop train line called the Outer Circle.
Whelan the Wrecker, a demolition company, placed 'Whelan is Here' signs on buildings it demolished, and its scrapyard was originally at the corner of Sydney Road and Hope Street.
The 1969 Melbourne Transport Plan also laid out new train lines, including the Frankston to Dandenong loop, but most were abandoned or still on the cards.
Up until the 1970s, Yarra Boulevard had no speed limit, as did any road in Victoria without street lights or dividing lines.
Melbourne is the only Australian city that still uses hook turns for cars, a practice other cities abandoned by the 1950s.
The Queen Victoria Market is the only remaining market of several that originally surrounded the Melbourne CBD.

The foundation stones of the State Library of Victoria and the University of Melbourne were laid on the same day, both founded predominantly by Sir Redmond Barry, who later sentenced Ned Kelly to death.
Melbourne's CBD streets named King and Queen are actually named after Governor King, King William IV, Queen Adelaide, and Elizabeth Bourke, not the monarchs.
The Yarra River as it exists today is a human construction, with the Immigration Museum once sitting right on its water's edge as the former Customs House.
South Melbourne was originally called Emerald Hill, Port Melbourne was Sandridge, and North Melbourne was Hotham Hill.
Exhibition Street in the CBD was formerly known as Stephen Street.
Southern Cross Station has the largest aluminium roof in Australia, covering 35,000 square metres.
Ned Kelly was hanged at the old Melbourne Jail.
The first espresso machine in Australia was put to use on Lygon Street, where Melbourne's coffee culture was born.
A stream flows underneath Elizabeth Street in the CBD, with a small outlet into the Yarra visible from the pedestrian bridge near Flinders Street Station.
The tram terminus at the Elizabeth Street and Flinders Street intersection is named after Sir Robert Risson, who resisted pressure to scrap Melbourne's trams.
Hamer Hall now stands on the site of Wirth's Circus, a permanent circus that was a major part of city entertainment, with a plaque marking the location.
John Pascoe Fawkner, an early colonial figure, founded Melbourne's first hotel and published its first newspaper by hand, and his name lives on in Fawkner, Fawkner Park, and Pascoe Vale.
The gold rush era made Melbourne one of the richest cities in the British Empire, at one stage only behind London and Liverpool.
Melbourne's CBD streets are laid out at an 8-degree angle from true north, a quirk that annoys architecture students.
The Yarra River around Richmond in the 1920s saw people throw sacks of unwanted puppies or kittens from bridges into the water.
Flagstaff Gardens is part of a former cemetery, meaning people are literally hanging out on top of dead bodies there.
The Crown Casino has a morgue and an illuminati tunnel system beneath it.
Footscray is where John Batman first landed, but the Maribyrnong River's salt water for 40km led them to settle further up at the Merri Creek.
Melbourne has produced three #1 overall NBA draft picks—Andrew Bogut, Kyrie Irving, and Ben Simmons—more than any other city in the last half century.

There used to be an airport next to where the West Gate Bridge now stands.

Melbourne experiences minor earthquakes.
On average, you are never more than 200 metres from a fox in Melbourne.

The longest running cinema in Melbourne is The Crazyhorse, operating continuously since the 1920s, with porn starting in the late 70s.
Albert Park lake and surroundings was once the tip for Melbourne's rubbish.
Melbourne ranks 24th on the list of cities with the most skyscrapers.
A large portion of Melbourne's south was swamp land until it was drained for farmland in the 1870s.

Melbourne was almost called Batmania, which would have made residents 'Batmanians'.

The city was briefly named Batmania after John Batman before being renamed Melbourne after the British Prime Minister, Lord Melbourne.

Mad Max once worked at the pumping station behind Science Works.

The IMAX screen in Melbourne is the biggest screen in the world.
Melbourne's first European settlers came from Tasmania, particularly Launceston.
The city was originally called Dootigala before being renamed Melbourne.
Some old people still refer to Melbourne as 'Batmania', a nod to an early alternative name.
The Yarra River's original waterfall was blown up in the 1880s to improve navigation, a fact often cited in local history.
Melbourne's exclusive rich men's club is said to hold sacred remains of First Australians.
There's a grotto with a fountain and memorial to JFK next to the Treasury building, though the reason for its existence remains unclear.
The free tram zone map is shaped like a submarine.
The Westend Market in Sunshine was also built upon a cemetery.

The 1893 Welfare Commission revealed that Melbourne's public health officer testified that post-mortems on over 500 children showed more than half had been murdered, a grim tidbit from the city's baby farming era.
London's grandeur is partly due to the Victorian goldrush, as most of the gold stored in the Melbourne Treasury was transported to England.
The deep tunnel system under Melbourne was used by 'interesting characters' for deals and business, and may still be in use in some form.
The Cave Clan, a group known for exploring underground tunnels and drains, has been active in Melbourne for decades.
The original burial records for the Queen Victoria Market cemetery were destroyed, so no one knows exactly how many bodies remain, but estimates range from 7,000 to 10,000.
A memorial cairn at Flagstaff Gardens, put up in 1870, marks the site of the earliest burials, which was unofficially known as 'Burial Hill'.
Advance Australia Fair was written by Peter McCormick on a bus on the way home from the Exhibition Centre in Melbourne.
The first Kmart in Australia opened at Burwood East in 1969.
St Kilda is named after a ship, Lady of St Kilda, not a saint.
The Treasury Building in Melbourne was built specifically to store gold.
Melbourne's original name, Bearbrass, was a mispronunciation of the Wurundjeri name Birrarung.
The 1956 Melbourne Olympics was the first to have an opening ceremony introducing all athletes.
Until 1966, it was illegal for pubs in Melbourne to be open after 6pm.
More NBA number one draft picks have been born in Melbourne than any other city, including Simmons, Irving, and Bogut.
The excess fill from digging the original sewerage system along Sydney Road was used to build the earthen terraces around Princes Park Football Ground.
City Hatters at Flinders Street Station has been in the same spot since the station opened in 1910.
Punt Road is named because it was the road to a punt crossing the Yarra River.
The Sandridge Bridge follows the line of Australia's first operational railway line, and one of its builders was John Monash.

In 1910, Harry Houdini jumped shackled in chains off Queens Bridge into the Yarra River.
The land where the MCG is located was once home to dinosaurs.
Little Lonsdale Street's top end was a community of immigrants, prostitution, and general scallywags with a notorious reputation.

Rocky Road was invented in Melbourne as a way to sell old chocolate stock to miners heading to the goldfields.
The original Melburnians were called 'cabbage patchers' because frequent burns made their skin look like cabbage.
Melbourne was almost named Batmania after John Batman, and also nearly called Bearbrass after a pub.
In 1917, a group of women led by suffragette Adela Pankhurst rampaged through Melbourne smashing buildings in protest over high bread and meat prices, an event known as the 1917 food riot.
Flinders Street Station is the busiest railway station in Australia and the entire Southern Hemisphere.
The corner of Collins Street and Elizabeth Street in Melbourne flooded so often it was nicknamed 'Lake Cashmore', and larrikins would push cops and stuck-up people into the water.
Melbourne was once called 'Smelbourne' because some parts of the city didn't get sewerage facilities until the 1960s.
Melbourne is often called the fox capital of the western world, with more foxes per square metre than London.
Quite a few buildings in Melbourne's city centre have long basements where people used to practice shooting in case of a Hun invasion, including one under Parliament House.
Melbourne's Pound Bend tunnel dates back to the mid-1800s and features redbrick and bluestone construction, MMBW worker graffiti from the 1940s, and Cave Clan tags from the 1980s-2000s.
The Queen Vic Market carpark was built on top of graves, with a plaque in the park noting some of the earliest settlers are buried there.
The Yarra River once had a waterfall that was blown up to improve navigation.
Melbourne's first porno shop was protested by a bizarre coalition of Nazis, radical feminists, and religious nutters.

The Salvation Army Limelight Department, operating in Melbourne from 1897 to 1910, was Australia's first film production company and produced the world's first multimedia presentation using moving picture film technology.
Swanston Street near Melbourne University used to be called Madeline Street.
Batman's son fell off the stones crossing the Yarra River and died.

Melbourne's hilly areas like Richmond and Fitzroy were highly desirable for residential use, while valley areas like Collingwood were kept for industrial purposes due to airflow and pollution concerns.
Melbourne's CBD east end, including Collins and Bourke Streets after Swanston, is built on top of old houses, creating a noticeable hill when walking up.
Elizabeth Street in Melbourne is built on top of a creek from the city's founding, which is why it is prone to flooding.
The first hydroelectric plant in Victoria was at Dights Falls near Clifton Hill, where a flour mill's turbines and generators from the late 1880s are still preserved.
Melbourne's Moomba festival name is derived from Aboriginal words meaning 'up your bum', as 'moom' means buttocks and '-ba' is a suffix for 'at' or 'in'.
A claypit quarry once operated in Brunswick, with remnants of quarry equipment still visible along the creek south of CERES.
Melbourne still has an ironclad ship visible from the coast, partially underwater but preserved.
The city's street order King, William, Queen, Elizabeth reflects a royal hierarchy, with Elizabeth Street named after a creek it was built over.
Melbourne's Flinders Street Station's ballroom is much smaller than commonly perceived.
The city's plans for Flinders Street Station were accidentally swapped with those for Bombay or Delhi, meaning each city received the other's intended building design.
Melbourne was initially deemed an illegal settlement by Sydney, but authorities couldn't stop it and instead tried to govern it.
Governor Bourke declared the land terra nullius to delegitimize Batman's treaty with native tribes, legally stripping them of property rights.
Melbourne's Elizabeth Street floods because it was built over a creek, a design flaw from the city's early days.
The Yarra River's waterfall at Dights Falls was used for the first hydroelectric plant in Victoria, with the original turbine housing still intact.
Melbourne's CBD has utility tunnels under it, but they are well secured and were easier to sneak into before 2001, with some sections bricked off after about 40 metres.
The suburb of Cremorne only officially existed since 1999, and its old railway station named 'Cremorne Station' is why East Richmond is called that despite being in Cremorne.
Altona: The Altona Homestead, built by Alfred Langhorne in the 1840s, still stands in Logan Reserve.
The Truganina Explosives Reserve, which operated from 1901 to 1958, is now a wetlands area with remnants of brick magazines.
Altona was a popular seaside resort until the 1960s, but many of its early houses were technically holiday shacks.
Armadale: The suburb's name is pronounced 'Ar-ma-dale', not 'Arm-a-dale' — a common mistake that locals are quick to correct.
Ascot Vale: The Flemington Meat Preserving Company in Ascot Vale produced powdered soup for Australian troops during World War I.
There are two Woolworths Metros in Ascot Vale — double the overpriced convenience for locals.
The Travancore Estate, once a prestigious subdivision, is now home to an Australian Catholic University campus.
Ashburton: Ashburton was identified as the centre of the metropolitan area based on 1991 census population data.
The suburb's name comes from Ashburton in Cork, Ireland, suggested by a local councillor in 1890.
A 2022 Reddit post reported a 'golden doughnut shaped object' flying over Ashburton; it was likely a Mylar balloon, but it sparked a fun local UFO scare.
Balwyn North: Balwyn North is home to the Greythorn and Bellevue localities, each with their own distinct village feel.
Blackburn: Blackburn was home to the first Open Air School in 1915, designed for inner-city children with poor health and nutrition.
The Blue Moon Fruit Co-operative, formed in 1930, exported fresh fruit from local orchards to England.
Braybrook: Braybrook was once part of the City of Sunshine, created from the Braybrook Shire in 1951.
Brighton: Brighton's bathing boxes were originally built in the 1850s and have been contentious ever since.
Broadmeadows: Broadmeadows was once a separate city until 1994, when it was merged into Hume City.
The suburb's name comes from the descriptive 'broad-meadows' plain country surveyed in 1850 — nothing to do with the broad beans some locals joke about.
Brunswick: The 1930s depression was so hard on Brunswick that roads like Hope and Albion streets were built by unemployed men on sustenance labour.
Brunswick East: The suburb's population is 30% overseas-born, with significant American, Canadian, and Brazilian communities — reflected in the local coffee culture.
Burnley: The Burnley group of train lines is the only one in Melbourne that still reverses direction in the city loop, causing daily confusion for commuters.
Carlton: Carlton has no train station — trams are the only rail, with routes 1, 6, and 96 running through.
Carlton's population is 55% born overseas, with Mandarin and Indonesian among the most over-represented languages.
Carnegie: A.V. Jennings, one of Australia's biggest builders, built his first 20 houses — the Hillcrest Estate — in Carnegie in 1933.
Caulfield North: The suburb's name comes from Baron Caulfield, an Irish peer, and 'North' distinguishes it from its southern neighbour.
Chadstone: In 1989, residents of east Chadstone successfully petitioned to have their area renamed East Malvern, desperate to escape the Chadstone name.
The Chadstone Dymocks is famous for wholesome meet-cutes — one Reddit user's chance encounter there went viral and spawned a cult-following thread.
Cheltenham: Cheltenham's name comes from the Cheltenham Inn, named after the owner's home town in England — not the racecourse.
The Cheltenham Cat Rescue adoption days are a beloved local institution, and the suburb's Russian-speaking community is 4.8 times the metro average.
Clifton Hill: The suburb has a higher proportion of American-born residents than most of Melbourne — 3.6 times the metro average.
Coburg: A 28-year-old dog tag from Broadmeadows was found on a roof in Coburg during a renovation, sparking a mystery that Reddit solved with theories ranging from bower birds to post-breakup property disputes.
Coburg North: Coburg North's water supply comes from a different reservoir than Coburg, which is why it was included in a boil-water alert while its southern neighbour wasn't.
Collingwood: Collingwood was one of the first places in the world where people 'barracked' for a footy team — the term comes from the Collingwood Rifles military unit.
Cranbourne: The Cranbourne racing complex is one of the largest training centres in Australia, hosting turf, harness, and greyhound racing.
Cranbourne's name may come from Viscount Cranbourne, son of the Marquess of Salisbury, or an English town of the same name.
Cremorne: Cremorne ranked #1 in Melbourne for cafe density, beating the CBD, Southbank, and South Melbourne.
East Richmond station is actually in Cremorne, but was named after Richmond because Cremorne didn't exist as a suburb when it was built.
Dandenong: Dandenong was nicknamed the 'gateway to Gippsland' after the Gippsland Road (now Princes Highway) was built in 1858, making it a staging post for Cobb & Co coaches.
Dandenong is home to people of 137 national origins, making it one of the most multicultural places in Australia.
The Dandenong stock market, once one of Victoria's main cattle markets, operated beside the railway station from 1958 until its closure in 1998.
Docklands: Docklands has no dedicated train station — the nearest is Southern Cross, a 10-15 minute walk away.
Doncaster: The suburb's population is 55% born overseas, with Persian, Cantonese, and Mandarin among the most over-represented languages.
East Melbourne: East Melbourne has a higher proportion of American-born residents than almost any other Melbourne suburb — 3.3 times the metro average.
The suburb's name comes from its position east of the CBD, but it was originally part of the 'Eastern Hill' area, which included parts of what is now the CBD.
The 1866 isometric map of Melbourne shows Fitzroy Gardens extending all the way to Victoria Parade — the park was much larger back then.
Elsternwick: The Elsternwick Club was formed in 1898 so Caulfield's 'more prosperous' residents could meet on 'socially acceptable terms'.
Eltham: The Eltham Copper butterfly, an endangered species, is found only in a few spots around the suburb.
Elwood: Elwood has no hotels—the only pub is in a distant corner—but it's had a thriving bar scene since gentrification.
The 246 bus is the only public transport that actually goes into Elwood, and it doesn't even go to the city.
Epping: The suburb was home to a man who built a tri-axle HQ Monaro ute from two cars — a local legend known as 'Siggy' who used it as his work vehicle for years.
Fawkner: Fawkner has the highest proportion of Italian-born residents of any Melbourne suburb (20% at the 1996 census).
Fitzroy: The Brunswick Street Oval was the former home of the Fitzroy Football Club, now the Brisbane Lions, and is still a beloved local park.
Fitzroy North: Fitzroy North is officially in both the City of Yarra and City of Merri-bek councils — one of the few suburbs split between two LGAs.
The suburb has a 'Hipster accent' according to r/melbourne — a distinct inner north-east way of speaking not found in West Brunswick.
A woman was charged with attempted murder after allegedly assaulting a jogger near Merri Creek — a story that shook the usually peaceful suburb.
Flemington: The Flemington Bridge station's design is based on an indigenous eel trap, a nod to the Kulin nations' connection to the Maribyrnong.
The touch-free crossing button in Flemington was installed so Orthodox Jews could cross on the Sabbath without pressing a mechanical button.
Footscray: Footscray was almost the site of Melbourne's CBD – the city was originally meant to be built west, but the ground wasn't stable enough.
The Footscray Hotel has a reputation as one of Melbourne's scummiest pubs, but it's also known for helping those in need, shunning developers to keep its doors open.
Frankston: Frankston was once considered as a site for Melbourne's main cemetery and crematorium, but Springvale was chosen instead.
DJ Carl Cox, the famous UK techno DJ, has made Frankston his home.
Glen Iris: The number 6 tram to Glen Iris was the setting of a viral r/Melbourne story about a Karen screaming 'IM THE LEAST RACIST PERSON YOULL EVER MEET' at a passenger who called out her racism.
Glen Waverley: The suburb is home to one of Melbourne's best-rated laksa spots, Laksa King, which has a loyal following that debates its Glen Waverley branch vs. the original Flemington one.
A single house in Glen Waverley once sold for $1.4 million unrenovated, proving that the 'affordable housing' map is a cruel joke.
Hampton: Hampton has a small but notable Russian-speaking community, spoken at 3.4 times the Melbourne average.
Hawthorn: Hawthorn was a city in its own right for over a century before merging into Boroondara in 1994 — it had its own town hall and civic pride.
The suburb's name comes from the hawthorn hedges that once lined the early roads, not from any bird.
Heidelberg: The first local government body in Victoria was the Heidelberg Road Trust, formed in 1841 to improve the road to Melbourne.
Hughesdale: Despite its small size, Hughesdale has seven mapped cafes, including the intriguingly named 'Temperance Society'.
The 2021 census recorded 7,563 residents, but the suburb's identity is so tied to Chadstone that some joke it's just the mall's overflow parking.
Ivanhoe: The Ivanhoe Hotel was built in the 1850s, making it one of the oldest buildings in the area.
The Ivanhoe Library has a cafe downstairs and allows you to eat your own food upstairs, as long as it doesn't smell.
Keilor: Caroline Chisholm's shelter sheds for gold rush families were built near Keilor village, encouraging women and children to follow their men to the diggings.
The suburb's apricot orchards were so famous in the 1880s that irrigation pioneer David Milburn turned them into a model for the whole district.
Keilor's population trebled between 1947 and 1954, thanks to cheap new houses and manufacturing jobs — and it's been a commuter haven ever since.
Kensington: A Carl's Jr dark kitchen operates in an industrial estate in Kensington, with no storefront — just a kitchen churning out burgers for Uber Eats.
Kew: NBA star Kyrie Irving was born in Kew.
Malvern: Malvern was once part of the Shire of Gardiner, named after the pioneer who overlanded cattle from NSW in 1836.
Maribyrnong: A Toyota satnav once listed 'Knifepoint' as a location in Maribyrnong, thanks to a prank on OpenStreetMap.
Mernda: Mernda's name comes from a Woiwurrung word meaning 'earth'.
The Mernda line is one of the few train lines in Melbourne that doesn't have any express services, making it one of the slowest ways to get to the city.
Middle Park: Middle Park's population is just 4,000, and the average house price is around $2.8 million.
The suburb's streetscapes are so intact they look straight out of the 1880s, like rings on a tree tracking Melbourne's growth.
Noble Park: The 1969 Melbourne Transport Plan proposed a massive freeway grid through the area — it was cancelled, which is why Noble Park's streets are so tangled.
North Melbourne: North Melbourne was once the most densely populated part of Melbourne during the 1880s land boom.
Northcote: The suburb was once home to a German settlement called Cawdortown, whose cemetery still exists as the German Cemetery.
Oak Park: The suburb's population is just over 6,700, but it has one of Melbourne's highest concentrations of Nepali speakers — 7 times the metro average.
Oakleigh: Oakleigh's name likely comes from Oakleigh Park in Hertfordshire, England, not from any local oak trees.
The suburb's population trebled between 1945 and 1961, driven by migrant hostels and new industry — by 1974, one local primary school had students from 24 nationalities.
Ormond: The suburb's Russian-speaking population is nine times the Melbourne average, a legacy of post-war migration.
Ormond's streetscape is so distinctly 1930s that locals use it to date Melbourne's growth rings.
Pakenham: Pakenham was once known as Longford, after an aristocratic English family, before the name changed to commemorate a general or a Dublin churchman.
Parkville: Parkville's population is over half under 34, with many residents being students at the University of Melbourne.
Point Cook: The RAAF base at Point Cook is the oldest continuously operating military airfield in the world.
Port Melbourne: The red ship seen in the time-lapse, the Far Saracen, helped with bushfire relief at Mallacoota in 2020.
Port Melbourne's population of 25-34 year olds grew by 76.5% between 1996 and 2000, signalling its rapid gentrification.
Prahran: The Prahran Town Hall on Chapel Street opened in 1861, and the suburb was proclaimed a city in 1879 — making it one of Melbourne's earliest established municipalities.
Preston: Preston Market has been around since 1970 and is considered one of Melbourne's best fresh food markets, drawing people from across the city.
Preston was declared a city in 1926, and its population boomed after the railway was electrified in 1921.
Princes Hill: The suburb has a population of just over 2,000 — smaller than many a single apartment block in the CBD.
Reservoir: Reservoir has a reservoir — the Edwardes Lake, which is actually a man-made lake on Edgars Creek, formed in part on land donated in 1916.
Richmond: Richmond was one of the first suburbs to establish municipal government, self-governing by 1855, and became a city in 1882.
The suburb's population was 40,000 by Federation, making it a self-sufficient community where most people lived and worked within its boundaries.
Ringwood: The name 'Ringwood' comes from a town in Hampshire, England, but an earlier name for the district was reportedly 'Ballyduffy'.
Ripponlea: Ripponlea's median house price is well over a million, but it has a population smaller than some apartment blocks in South Yarra.
South Melbourne: The first railway in Australia ran from Melbourne to Port Melbourne in 1854, branching off at Ferrars Street to St Kilda — now the light rail route.
The suburb's population peaked at 47,000 in the 1920s, but has since dropped to around 11,500 as housing quality rose and industry moved out.
South Yarra: South Yarra's elevated parts were once dotted with mansions like Como House, whose gardens were gradually subdivided into the apartment blocks you see today.
Southbank: The NGV's Winter Masterpieces and the Melbourne Recital Centre's acoustics (designed by the same team as Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie) are world-class cultural draws.
Spotswood: Spotswood's population is just 2,820, making it one of Melbourne's smallest inner suburbs — but it packs in 13 parks and 3 schools.
Springvale: The suburb's library lets you borrow up to 40 items at once, a fact locals are very proud of.
St Albans: The suburb was named after St Albans in Hertfordshire by Alfred Padley, who had family connections there — not because of any local saint.
There's a Big 4 caravan park in St Albans that a regional Victorian family described as 'an eye opener' — but they admitted it was 'just a suburb'.
St Kilda: The St Kilda Football Club left its home in 1965 and immediately won its first and only AFL Grand Final — a premiership drought that continues to this day.
The visual effects for many Marvel movies are made in St Kilda — Method Studios, on St Kilda Road, has done VFX for a heap of Hollywood blockbusters.
St Kilda West: St Kilda West is only 5 km from the CBD but has no train station—just trams and the beach.
A 1-bedroom apartment in 'East Middle Park' (a.k.a. St Kilda West) can go for $350k, a bargain compared to Brisbane's $600k.
Sunbury: The local name for Jacksons Creek might be 'sunburra', possibly the origin of the suburb's name.
Sunshine: The suburb's population is 48% born overseas, with Nepali spoken at 8.3 times the metro rate.
Sunshine North: Sunshine North has a higher Maltese-born population than almost anywhere else in Melbourne — 11 times the metro average.
Thornbury: Thornbury's postcode 3071 was once N17, part of Melbourne's old English-style postal system that radiated out from the Hoddle Grid.
Toorak: Toorak has the highest percentage of children attending private schools in Melbourne.
The 'Toorak side of Reservoir' is a real estate myth — the actual suburb is Preston or Coburg North, but REAs love to pretend otherwise.
In the 1960s, Toorak residents spoke with noticeably posh accents, as captured in a vintage newsreel that amused Reddit.
Travancore: The suburb has no verified restaurants on OpenStreetMap — only 3 Indian restaurants and 3 cafes — so locals walk to Newmarket for a decent feed.
West Footscray: West Footscray is home to one of Melbourne's few remaining Nissen huts, repurposed after WWII as migrant accommodation.
West Melbourne: The suburb's postcode 3003 includes Flagstaff Gardens, Queen Victoria Market, and the Melbourne Remand Centre — a strange mix of park, market, and jail.
West Melbourne has a Korean population 7.5 times the metro average, making it a hidden hub for Korean food and culture.
Williamstown: Ned Kelly played six games for Williamstown Football Club.
Australia's first telegraph line connected Melbourne and Williamstown in 1854.
The Alfred Graving Dock, completed in 1874, was reputedly the largest dry dock in the southern hemisphere.
The old Williamstown Rifle Range was decommissioned and redeveloped into housing in the 1990s.
Windsor: Windsor station opened in 1859, making it one of Melbourne's oldest suburban stations — it predates the suburb's official status as a distinct place.
Lindsay Fox, the trucking magnate, grew up in Windsor on the wrong side of the tracks — his dad ran a sly grog shop out the back of their house.
Yarraville: The suburb's first land sale in 1859 was launched with a banquet extolling views of Melbourne — but without a station until 1871, it stayed a quarry town for decades.
Yarraville was once home to Australia's first fertiliser factory, thanks to local bone mills and acid works that drove the noxious trades industry.
